title: Bidāyat al-Ḥikma
author: Sayyid Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
description: The first systematic course in the two-book sequence. This entry provides an original reading guide, a twelve-stage comparison with Nihāya, and details of Qarāʾī’s published English translation. The full Arabic–English text is awaiting a supplied or clearly reusable Arabic source.

editorialStatus.method: Original editorial guidance; no full authorial Arabic text or published English translation reproduced.

sources.title: Bidāyat al-ḥikma — Arabic contents
sources.description: Reference for stage order and chapter counts. Availability online is not treated as an open republication licence.

sources.title: ʿAlī Qulī Qarāʾī, The Elements of Islamic Metaphysics (Bidāyat al-Ḥikmah)
sources.description: Published English translation of Bidāya, ICAS Press; the publisher lists a fully revised second edition. Bibliographic reference only: its English wording is not reproduced here, and no complete comparison against it is claimed.

stages.title: Existence in Itself and in Another
Knowledge, the Knower, and the Known

units.title: Bidāya, Nihāya, and the Existing English Translation
units.arabic: هذا دليل قراءة تحريري، وليس ترجمة لمتن بداية الحكمة. يوضح ترتيب مباحث الكتاب وعلاقته بنهاية الحكمة، ويحيل إلى الترجمة الإنجليزية المنشورة. لم يُدرج المتن العربي أو ترجمة كاملة له في هذه الصفحة بعد.
units.english:
Bidāyat al-Ḥikma is the earlier systematic course in Ṭabāṭabāʾī’s two-book sequence. Nihāyat al-Ḥikma returns to the same broad architecture at a more demanding level. Both have twelve stages, but their order and internal chapter divisions differ. Bidāya has 110 numbered chapters; Nihāya has 130.

A published English translation of Bidāya is available: The Elements of Islamic Metaphysics, translated by Sayyid ʿAlī Qulī Qarāʾī, ICAS Press. The publisher lists a fully revised second edition with terminology notes and a glossary. Its wording is not reproduced in this reader.

The sections below are original editorial reading prompts, not a substitute translation of the book. A full new translation is awaiting a supplied Arabic source or a clearly reusable Arabic witness. The linked Nihāya edition provides its own separately identified working translation.

For comparison, match each topic across the books rather than advancing through identical stage or chapter numbers. The study guide also explains the usual progression into Mullā Ṣadrā’s Asfār and the separate theoretical ʿirfān sequence.

notes.text: Published English: The Elements of Islamic Metaphysics, trans. ʿAlī Qulī Qarāʾī, ICAS Press.
The guide’s stage correspondence is structural. It does not assert that arguments or individual chapters are identical.

units.title: Existence: General Questions — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة I: عدد فصولها 12. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة I من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Begin by distinguishing a concept from the reality to which it applies, and existence from what a thing is. Keep the primacy of existence and its gradation separate: the first asks what is concrete; the second asks how one reality admits different degrees. These are related theses with different argumentative tasks.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage I, 12 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage I.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage I in the companion reader.

units.title: Mental and External Existence — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة II: عدد فصولها 1. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة III من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Ask how something can be present to knowledge without producing its ordinary external effects. The distinction between modes of existence is crucial: thinking about fire does not make the mind physically hot. When comparing the two books, match this stage with Nihāya III rather than with the same Roman numeral.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage II, 1 numbered chapter; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage III.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage III in the companion reader.

units.title: Existence in Itself and in Another — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة III: عدد فصولها 3. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة II من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Keep “in itself,” “for itself,” and “through itself” distinct. They answer different questions about conceptual independence, qualification of a subject, and dependence upon a cause. An English translation that replaces all three with “independent” makes the arguments harder to follow. The corresponding discussion is Nihāya II.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage III, 3 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage II.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage II in the companion reader.

units.title: Necessity, Possibility, and Impossibility — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة IV: عدد فصولها 9. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة IV من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Read the modal vocabulary together with the theory of causation. A thing can be contingent in itself while necessary through a complete cause. Reconstruct each claim by specifying whether the necessity or possibility belongs intrinsically, through another, or by comparison. Do not treat “possible” as merely “not yet actual.”

Structural reference: Bidāya stage IV, 9 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage IV.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage IV in the companion reader.

units.title: Quiddity and Its Properties — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة V: عدد فصولها 8. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة V من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
The guiding question is what a thing is, considered apart from an additional assertion that it exists. Track genus, differentia, species, universality, and individuation. Ask which distinctions concern concepts and which are supposed to mark concrete divisions. This prevents a logical analysis of a definition from becoming an unsupported claim about separate things.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage V, 8 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage V.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage V in the companion reader.

units.title: The Ten Categories — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة VI: عدد فصولها 11. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة VI من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Use a clear account of substance and accident before moving into the traditional category scheme. Distinguish prime matter from ordinary physical material and form from outward shape. Nihāya devotes more numbered chapters to this stage, but chapter totals alone do not measure the depth or independence of individual arguments.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage VI, 11 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage VI.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage VI in the companion reader.

units.title: Cause and Effect — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة VII: عدد فصولها 11. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة VIII من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Distinguish a complete cause from one contributing condition, and causal dependence from temporal precedence. When reading objections to regress, determine what kind of ordered dependence is at issue. A series of earlier events and a hierarchy of presently dependent causes should not be assumed to be the same kind of series.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage VII, 11 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage VIII.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage VIII in the companion reader.

units.title: Unity and Multiplicity — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة VIII: عدد فصولها 10. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة VII من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Follow the different senses of unity, identity, predication, and opposition. Primary predication and common predication can yield different judgments without contradiction because they consider different relations. Compare each apparently incompatible statement only after specifying the relevant sense of identity and the respects in which the predication is made.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage VIII, 10 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage VII.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage VII in the companion reader.

units.title: Priority, Posteriority, Beginninglessness, and Origination — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة IX: عدد فصولها 3. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة X من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Do not assume that every “before” is temporal. The classification separates several kinds of priority; correspondingly, origination can concern dependence rather than a first date. For comparison, turn to Nihāya X, which has eight numbered chapters in this area. Keep its technical uses of dahr and sarmad distinct from ordinary elapsed time.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage IX, 3 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage X.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage X in the companion reader.

units.title: Potentiality and Actuality — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة X: عدد فصولها 16. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة IX من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Track what changes, the respect in which it changes, and what accounts for continuity. In substantial motion, the identity of the subject is a philosophical problem requiring argument. Distinguish motion considered as traversal from the moving thing’s intermediate state between endpoints. The corresponding stage in Nihāya is IX.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage X, 16 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage IX.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage IX in the companion reader.

units.title: Knowledge, the Knower, and the Known — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة XI: عدد فصولها 12. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة XI من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Keep knowledge by presence distinct from acquired knowledge, and conception distinct from assent. “Acquired” names a mode of knowing through a form; it does not always mean knowledge obtained by deliberate study. When comparing the books, follow the arguments and subdivisions, since identical stage numbers do not guarantee identical chapter numbers.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage XI, 12 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage XI.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage XI in the companion reader.

units.title: The Necessary Existent — Reading Prompts
units.arabic: دليل تحريري للمرحلة XII: عدد فصولها 14. يقابل هذا الموضوع إجمالًا المرحلة XII من نهاية الحكمة. هذه إرشادات للقراءة والمقارنة، وليست نص المؤلف أو ترجمةً له.
units.english:
Read the final theological discussion as dependent on the preceding metaphysics. Distinguish proving necessary existence from determining unity, attributes, and action. A critical reading should identify the earlier premises each conclusion needs and the objections it answers. Nihāya’s corresponding stage has twenty-four numbered chapters and requires a separate argument-by-argument comparison.

Structural reference: Bidāya stage XII, 14 numbered chapters; corresponding topic in Nihāya stage XII.

notes.text: Consult Nihāya stage XII in the companion reader.

glossary.definition: The act or reality of being. Distinguish the concept of existence from the extra-mental reality to which it applies.
That which exists. “Being” can name an existent, so the translation usually reserves “existence” for wujūd.
What a thing is, considered as the answer to “What is it?” Its conceptual distinction from existence is central to the work.
The thesis that existence is primary in concrete realization, while quiddities are abstracted from it. This is an ontological thesis, not a claim that ordinary things are imaginary.
A context-sensitive term. A quiddity’s derivative status, an abstract philosophical concept, and a practical convention should not automatically receive the same English rendering.
Unity of a reality across different degrees, where the basis of difference returns to the basis of agreement. Distinguish this from mere ambiguity of a word.
The intelligible meaning and what it applies to. Distinct concepts need not entail distinct externally existing things.
The domain in relation to which a judgment is true; it should not automatically be reduced to a separate physical object.
Existence whose reality is dependent rather than independently established. Attend to the distinction between a proposition’s copular relation and an effect’s dependence upon its cause.

glossary.english: In itself / for itself / through itself
glossary.definition: Three distinct relations. The translation retains their differences rather than flattening all of them into “independent.”
The mode in which something is present as known without necessarily producing the external effects associated with its extra-mental existence.
The basic modalities. Imkān is “contingency” when contrasted with intrinsic necessity, but “possibility” is preferable in many other modal contexts.
Intrinsic status must be distinguished from status derived from another. A contingent thing can become necessary through its complete cause without becoming intrinsically necessary.
A substance is not in a subject independent of it; an accident exists in such a subject. This distinction does not make accidents unreal.
Matter is the receptive principle and form the actuality through which it is determined. Prime matter is not simply a small physical particle.
Predication considered through identity of meaning or quiddity. Distinguish it from a predication concerning concrete instances.
Predication grounded in unity of instance despite conceptual difference. The literal rendering “industrial predication” is avoided.
The explanatory dependence of an effect upon a cause need not imply that the cause precedes it in time.
The total causal condition upon whose realization the effect necessarily follows. An incomplete cause alone does not suffice for the effect.
Bringing something into existence, distinguished from making an already posited thing possess an additional determination.
A receptive possibility and its realization. Quwwa also means an active power; fiʿl also means an act. The contrast determines the translation.
Change in the existence of material substance itself, rather than only in its accidental states. Its subject and continuity require separate argument.
Two considerations of motion: the moving thing’s state between endpoints, and its successive passage through the course.
Time measures motion. Dahr and sarmad name technical atemporal relations of coexistence. Rendering all three with ordinary temporal language obscures the argument.
Whether existence is or is not preceded by nonexistence. The relevant kind of precedence must be specified; intrinsic origination is not simply a date in the past.
Knowledge in which the known itself is present to the knower, rather than known through a separately mediating acquired form.
Knowledge through the presence of a form representing what is known. “Acquired” here names a mode of knowledge, not necessarily the result of deliberate learning.
Apprehending a meaning and assenting to a judgment. These should be kept distinct when reading the account of acquired knowledge.
The act or principle of intellection, the one knowing, and what is intelligibly known. “Knower” is used where the broader English sense fits the argument.
That whose existence is intrinsically necessary. The final stage argues about its existence, unity, attributes, and acts.
